Q: Splunk starts again immediately after stopping the service on Linux A:

How can I find out what is restarting Splunk after I stop it?

  1. For "the usual methods", make sure that you have the correct service name in the first place. No point in trying to stop or mask a service, if it doesn't exist. (Note that service names are case-sensitive – and not necessarily matching the process/binary name – so 'splunkd' and 'Splunkd' are not the same.)

    Also make sure the stop job actually completed and isn't just sitting in the job queue (systemctl list-jobs).

    So always do a systemctl status <name> before and/or after the operation, to see if your command at least did its immediate task. For example, after you did a systemctl stop and the service is running again, you should be expecting to see "active since 5 seconds ago". Whereas if you stop a service, but it says "active since 2 months ago", then you didn't actually stop it at all.

  2. In the same systemctl status Splunkd, pay attention to the TriggeredBy field. Some services use "socket activation" where systemd (or historically inetd/xinetd) holds on to the listening sockets, so that whenever something else tries to connect, this immediately triggers a service startup.

    So if splunkd happens to be socket-activated and there is a consumer of splunkd always re-connecting it, it will keep causing the service to start again.

  3. Watch the system logs, i.e. journalctl -f. There may be messages related to this, e.g. from crond or something such. (Absence of messages – i.e. absence of the usual "Started splunk.service" – is also relevant, although it'd give you the same information as the next point.)

  4. Use systemctl status <pid> (specifically PID, not name!) to see which cgroup or systemd unit the daemon is started from.

    You might find that it is actually running from something weird like supervisord.service, or you might find that it is running from within a user session where some weird script is running inside of a tmux.

    cat /proc/<pid>/cgroup will give a similar result.

  5. Use ps axf, pstree, htop to see what the parent process of splunkd is.

    This somewhat complements the previous point. Sometimes the cgroup hierarchy is enough to reveal the culprit, sometimes the process hierarchy tells you more.

    If it's systemd(pid1), that doesn't mean much – the original parent may have exited, and the daemon reparented to pid1. But if it's e.g. crond or supervisord, now you have a lead.

    There are also tools which let you watch the spawning of processes in real time: forkstat, extrace, and I think also execsnoop from bpf-tools.

Also, what is the correct way to completely stop Splunk and prevent it from starting again automatically?

The "correct" way depends entirely on what was starting it automatically (i.e. you need to make that thing stop trying to start Splunk, which is a different matter than merely preventing it from starting Splunk). Therefore impossible to answer unless you solve the previous question first.

The "general" way is to remove the executable file that's being started (or rename it to something like 'Splunk.disabled'). Keep in mind that if you do this, something will still keep trying to start it automatically – and might start flooding your logs if it doesn't have a rate-limit – this method merely guarantees that it will never succeed, not that it will stop trying.

Q: i want to integrate ai into my food delivery logistics platform, how do i start A:

Just to clarify, you only want a chat bot that helps customers, not an AI agent. So while I understand you need/seek code and possibly CI/CD setup, until you reach that point, IMO you'll need to first understand the difference and then start a small design and analysis document where you need to specify your expectations (i.e. what you assume or want or whatever, the LLM to do). After that, you'll need to ALWAYS grant exactly the access it needs, nothing more.

For example, consider only logged in users can use the chatbot (or if you want it available to others that are not authenticated - which I don't recommend, have restricted access, but the issue with this is there might be a 0.0000001% chance of either hallucination or accessing a separate user's account data, depending on how you setup the comms between the LLM and your components, such as DB, webapp, etc.).

So from there, you'd prolly need to see what order is in progress or if you want some sort of complaint system, then the LLM would need to see past/finalized orders too.

Here is where it gets tricky: if you want it to only give advice (i.e. "you have some sort of issue, in order to fix it do this, that, x, y"), then this is enough. If you want the AI to do automated stuff like if the payment fails and the customer wants to retry, cancel the order, add something else, whatever other crazy stuff from an LLM prompt, then you can't do it. You'll need an AI Agent. And this is where it gets tricky as you'll need to make sure it has only read-only rights, unless you want to have some nasty surprises.

Back to customer help-only, The LLM will need to be trained on your shop (or whatever it is) mechanics/flows/internal procedures, meaning FAQs, user manuals, possibly SOME internal employee policies/procedures (also be careful with this, as it might expose confidential things). For instance how to cancel an order manually, how to do X, Y, Z (these are usually in FAQs or employee training procedures/instructions/manuals).

Then you have the see what model you need (or want) which can either be a SaaS (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.), or your own (that you deploy on-prem if you have a good server setup or on a PaaS). When I mean "your own" I don't literally mean "one made by you", but there are models (open-source or commercial) that have minimal training and are targeted at businesses that would train it for whatever they need to do.

The difference is, and I kid you not, if you'll use Claude or ChatGPT a user can literally ask it "how do I make an omelette" or even "how do I fix this C++/java/C#/python error?" and it would give the recipe and instructions or steps to fix the coding error. While it might seem funny to you, remember this does cost you usage. And the total usage cost might not the one you had in mind.

Then you'd need to take into account languages. Because you don't know what customers you have (consider tourists or if you expand abroad).

My point is, before you ask "I want code and advice on how to integrate", I think you need to plan this first. It's not quite "drag and drop" or "plug 'n' play" (depending on your age, you might get the references). Normally you'd need an architect, a technical analyst, a dev, obviously some legal guys that know privacy policies and AI Act (this also depends on your location as GDPR might be a factor or the AI act might not be) and obviously liability (remember that the chat bot must explicitly say they are an LLM, they might be beta and they might make mistakes unless you want serious legal issues - technically speaking, if you opt for a SaaS like ChatGPT, there are also some "less fortunate situations" surrounding it, security guys, network guys, obviously some people that know cloud infrastructure and the list goes on.

And obviously the access to data that it has should only be limited, i.e. not have data about names, addresses, payment (card PAN, CCV, etc.), profiling and so on. While ChatGPT is as secure as it can be, it had some issues:

  • 2023 Incident 768: ChatGPT Reportedly Implicated in Samsung Data Leak of Source Code and Meeting Notes or Inside ChatGPT Data Breach (March 2023): What Happened?
  • 2024 ChatGPT leak exposes private conversations and login credentials! Know what happened | Tech News (HT Tech)
  • 2025 OpenAI confirms ChatGPT data breach. Here is everything we know
  • 2026 ChatGPT Data Leakage via a Hidden Outbound Channel in the Code Execution Runtime or OpenAI Fixes Critical ChatGPT Data Leak Flaw & Codex GitHub Token Vulnerability, Raising Broader AI Security Concerns

So if I am to just answer you on how do I start?, the answer is: "planning first, analysis next, etc.". Oh, I didn't even mention you'll need a separate budget for this. So there's also that.

And keep in mind we didn't even reach the code part yet.
